paras: The 1903 whitecap attacks in Franklin and Amite counties, Mississippi, were night assaults by bands of "whitecaps" on Black residents of the two counties in late May 1903. In Franklin County the band fired fifty shots into the house of a Black man named Dillon, and in Amite County it shot a Black man who broke away when they tried to whip him. Mississippi papers reported the attacks as a renewal of "whitecapping outrages" that circuit courts had already tried to suppress.

Whitecapping had been active in Franklin and Amite counties before 1903, and the circuit courts had dealt "stern treatment" to earlier offenders. According to the Hattiesburg Daily Progress, Judge Powell and other judges had warned the whitecappers and "almost pleaded with them" to stop. The Water Valley Progress described the bands' purpose as driving "reputable negro tenants" out of the two counties.

About three weeks before the attack, Dillon, a Black man living in the McCall Creek neighborhood of Franklin County, had been warned to leave the neighborhood and had not done so. On a Saturday night, which a Jackson dispatch dated June 2 implies was about May 30, the whitecaps came to his house and fired fifty shots into it. The people inside "had narrow escapes from being killed," and no one there was reported hurt.

In Amite County whitecaps visited a Black man on the Wilson place intending to give him a thrashing. He pulled free of their grasp and ran, and one of the party fired on him. Seven buckshot lodged in his leg and a pistol ball grazed him, across the chin in the Hattiesburg text and across the hip in the Brandon text. The reports do not give the date of the Amite attack or the man's name.

No report of arrests, an investigation or a trial for these attacks appears in the coverage found. The Hattiesburg Daily Progress urged the next circuit court to "apply the law vigorously" against the whitecappers. By February 1904 the Atlanta Independent reported that Black laborers had steadily left Franklin, Amite and parts of Lincoln counties and that the three counties lacked "at least 80 per cent" of the labor they needed.

The detailed account came from a single Jackson dispatch, which the Hattiesburg Daily Progress printed on June 2 under the headline "WHITECAPPERS AGAIN." The Brandon News carried the same text on June 4, adding the first name "West" for Dillon, and the Water Valley Progress cut it to one line in its "Mississippi Matters" column on June 6. None of these papers named the attackers, and only the Water Valley item stated the bands' aim of driving Black tenants out.

The white papers treated the attacks as lawlessness rather than as justified, calling them "outrages." On its editorial page the Hattiesburg Daily Progress wrote that leniency toward whitecappers was "like being linient with a rattlesnake" and that the courts should teach them a lesson.

No Black-press report of the May 1903 attacks was found. Eight months later the Atlanta Independent, under the headline "WHITECAPS REAP WHIRLWIND," described whitecapping in Franklin County as "lawless conduct" by white men claiming to enforce "law and order." Its emphasis fell on the result: farmers in the county could not induce Black laborers to come "for love or money," even at "fancy wages."

The two full printings of the dispatch disagree on where the pistol ball struck the Amite man, the Hattiesburg Daily Progress saying his chin and the Brandon News his hip; neither text is clearly the better copy.

accounts.label: Jackson dispatch
accounts.gist: Whitecaps fired fifty shots into Dillon's house near McCall Creek on Saturday night after he ignored a warning to leave, and in Amite County shot a Black man who broke away when they tried to thrash him.

accounts.label: State news brief
accounts.gist: Whitecappers in Amite and Franklin were again shooting into the houses of 'reputable negro tenants' to drive them out of the counties.

accounts.label: Atlanta Independent
accounts.gist: A year of whitecapping in Franklin, Amite and Lincoln counties had driven Black labor away, leaving the counties short of workers.

framing.detail: The Hattiesburg Daily Progress headed the news 'WHITECAPPERS AGAIN', called the attacks 'outrages', and editorially compared leniency toward whitecappers to leniency 'with a rattlesnake'.
The Brandon News ran the dispatch without comment, and the Water Valley Progress reduced it to one line among state items, calling the targets 'reputable negro tenants'.
The Atlanta Independent, under 'WHITECAPS REAP WHIRLWIND', described the whitecapping as 'lawless conduct' by white men and its result as a labor famine.
